### TAG-199: Matterscript Developer's Guide

**Status:** ⬜ Not started

## Software Notes

Yes. Looking at the book as a whole, I think you're at a **very interesting inflection point**. The first four parts establish *why MatterScript should exist*; Part V is where the reader finally sees the language become concrete.

I would not radically reorganize the book. I would **continue the trajectory you've already established**, but make the transition from geometry → physical computation → compiler/runtime → complete systems increasingly explicit.

## The trajectory I see

The book currently has something like this underlying arc:

```
PART I
Rethink computation
        │
        ▼
PART II
Computation is a property of a physical/computational universe
        │
        ▼
PART III
Asynchronous computation changes the programming model
        │
        ▼
PART IV
MatterScript can learn and construct models of matter
        │
        ▼
PART V
Geometry becomes code
        │
        ▼
PART VI
Code becomes physical systems
        │
        ▼
PART VII
Space and time become programming primitives
        │
        ▼
PART VIII
The language becomes a compiler/toolchain
        │
        ▼
PART IX
The compiled system becomes a runtime
        │
        ▼
PART X
The runtime becomes a world model
        │
        ▼
PART XI
Multiple machines become one distributed
space-time computational system
        │
        ▼
PART XII
Complete systems
```

That's a **very strong book architecture**.

The important thing now is not to make every part increasingly abstract. Instead, I would make the book increasingly **concrete and demonstrable** as it progresses.

---

# Part V — Geometry Becomes Code

You're currently here.

And I think the geometry sequence we just developed is exactly the right foundation:

```
01 Spatial Domains
02 Vertices
03 Edges
04 Loops
05 Faces
06 Meshes
07 Cell Placement
08 Conformal Projection
09 Delay Synthesis
10 Sensor Placement
11 Hardware Fidelity
```

The first six chapters answer:

> **How do you represent physical space?**

```
domain
  ↓
point
  ↓
edge
  ↓
loop
  ↓
face
  ↓
mesh
```

Then the second half asks:

> **What does it mean to compute inside that space?**

```
mesh
 ↓
placement
 ↓
projection
 ↓
time
 ↓
sensing
 ↓
hardware
```

That distinction is important.

I would **finish Part V before moving on**. It gives the reader a complete conceptual journey from:

> "MatterScript can describe a point"

to:

> "MatterScript can describe a physical computational substrate."

And that's a major payoff.

---

# Part VI — Building Physical Systems

This is where I think the book should stop talking primarily about *geometry* and start talking about **systems**.

The reader has now learned that a surface can become a mesh and that computation can be associated with physical locations.

Now we ask:

> What can we actually build?

I envision this part progressing roughly:

```
Physical primitives
      ↓
components
      ↓
interconnect
      ↓
devices
      ↓
controllers
      ↓
sensors
      ↓
actuators
      ↓
complete physical system
```

This is where your HackerFab work becomes particularly important.

I would expect chapters around concepts like:

* physical components
* hardware targets
* sensors and actuators
* generated hardware
* FPGA / asynchronous logic
* embedded runtimes
* physical I/O
* fabrication interfaces
* measurement

The reader should leave Part VI thinking:

> **This isn't merely a language for describing physical things. It can describe systems that actually exist.**

---

# Part VII — Programming Space-Time

This is where the book can return to the deeper programming-language question.

By now the reader has experienced the consequences of treating space as a first-class computational dimension.

Now you can formally say:

> What happens when **time and space are both part of the program?**

This is where concepts like:

```
time
space
causality
locality
placement
delay
events
processes
```

can be unified.

I would make this part feel almost like the culmination of the language-design argument.

The progression becomes:

```
ordinary programming

    computation
         ↓
      execution


MatterScript

    computation
       ↙   ↘
   space    time
       ↘   ↙
      causality
```

This is also where your distinction between **tokens rather than variables**, **events rather than execution**, and **placement as frozen knowledge** can really pay off.

---

# Part VIII — Compilers and Code Generation

At this point, the reader has enough conceptual machinery to ask:

> How does this actually become a machine?

Now we descend into implementation.

This is where I would get very technical.

Something like:

```
MatterScript
     ↓
Parser
     ↓
AST
     ↓
Resolution
     ↓
Matter IR
     ↓
Optimization
     ↓
Target lowering
     ↓
VHDL / POSIX / mesh / hardware / ...
```

This part should explain that MatterScript isn't merely a DSL that emits one particular output.

It is becoming a **multi-target intermediate representation**.

That makes your existing work on:

* IPL
* spatial resolution
* VHDL generation
* PLY generation
* `@target`
* runtime boundaries
* generated hardware descriptions

fit together naturally.

### One thing I'd particularly emphasize

I think the compiler section should eventually introduce the concept:

> **MatterScript source describes relationships; the compiler decides how those relationships become machinery.**

That's a powerful distinction.

---

# Part IX — Runtimes

Then comes the question:

> What happens after compilation?

This is where your "runtime boundary" idea becomes central.

The architecture becomes:

```
Source
  ↓
Compiler
  ↓
Compiled Matter
  ↓
Runtime Boundary
  ↓
Physical / computational environment
```

And now you can introduce the idea that compiled MatterScript can potentially be:

* executed locally
* transmitted
* instantiated on another machine
* mapped onto another physical substrate
* adapted to different capabilities

This is where your idea of **"teleporting machinery"** becomes much more than a metaphor.

The runtime can become a receiver of *machinery descriptions*, not merely executable instructions.

That sets up Part X beautifully.

---

# Part X — World Modeling

This is where I think the book can become genuinely distinctive.

The runtime isn't merely executing a program.

It has:

```
state
geometry
time
sensors
models
events
causal relationships
```

Now introduce the idea of the **world model**.

And this is where the MatterScript + NKS + cellular-automata + learning work can converge.

The architecture becomes:

```
WORLD
  │
  ├── observe
  │
  ▼
MODEL
  │
  ├── infer
  │
  ▼
PREDICTION
  │
  ├── act
  │
  ▼
WORLD
```

That gives you the closed loop:

> **MatterScript doesn't merely describe a world. It can participate in a system that observes, models, predicts, and changes that world.**

This is a natural home for your theory-free/model-free inference ideas.

---

# Part XI — Distributed Space-Time Systems

Once you've established one physical computational system, the obvious next question is:

> What happens when there are many?

Now the architecture expands:

```
             SPACE-TIME SYSTEM
                    │
       ┌────────────┼────────────┐
       ▼            ▼            ▼
    Machine A    Machine B    Machine C
       │            │            │
       └────────────┼────────────┘
                    │
             shared causality
```

This is where your ideas around:

* intermittent synchronization
* high-resolution local time
* distributed physical state
* edge computation
* asynchronous systems
* spatial locality
* long-timespan sensing

can all converge.

And importantly, you don't have to fall back into the conventional distributed-computing model of:

```
server ↔ client
```

The conceptual model can instead be:

> **a distributed physical system whose components occupy different regions of space-time.**

That is much more consistent with the rest of the book.

---

That final project could serve as the practical synthesis of the entire book.

# The really interesting part

There is a deeper trajectory underneath all of this.

I think the book is gradually moving through **five different meanings of "program."**

```
1. A PROGRAM AS INSTRUCTIONS
        ↓
2. A PROGRAM AS RELATIONSHIPS
        ↓
3. A PROGRAM AS GEOMETRY
        ↓
4. A PROGRAM AS PHYSICAL MACHINERY
        ↓
5. A PROGRAM AS A MODEL OF A WORLD
```

And then Part XI takes the final step:

```
A PROGRAM AS A DISTRIBUTED WORLD
```

That's much more ambitious than "here's another programming language."

---

## And this is why Part V matters so much

The geometry chapters we're writing right now may initially look like implementation details:

```
Vertices
Edges
Loops
Faces
Meshes
```

But they're actually the **hinge of the entire book**.

Before Part V:

```
MatterScript
     ↓
an alternative way to express computation
```

After Part V:

```
MatterScript
     ↓
computation
     +
space
     +
time
```

And then:

```
space + time + computation
          ↓
     physical systems
          ↓
       runtimes
          ↓
     world models
          ↓
 distributed physical computation
```

So I would **not rush through Part V**. I'd make the geometry → mesh → placement transition extremely solid.

And after `Meshes`, **Cell Placement is the crucial next chapter**. That's where the book stops saying *"we can represent physical space"* and starts demonstrating *"we can put computation into physical space."*

That is the moment the title **MatterScript: A Programmer's Guide to Space-Time Computing** really starts to become literal.
